result: The authors developed a novel bimanual stick manipulation task where participants manipulated a virtual stick held with both hands to reach targets with the stick tip. This task creates redundancy because the same tip position can be achieved with different stick angles, allowing investigation of both end-effector relevant (tip position) and end-effector irrelevant (stick angle) perturbations.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the novel task design. Reviewer 2 states 'the authors have developed a novel bimanual task that allows them to study how the sensorimotor control system deals with redundancy' and notes it 'provides a very fruitful and important framework.' Reviewer 3 calls it 'an innovative bimanual stick manipulation task' and Reviewer 1 describes it as 'a new task offering a myriad of possible coordination patterns.' The editor confirms 'the evidence supporting the authors' claims is convincing.'

result: During baseline movements, participants consistently employed a stereotypical strategy where stick-tilt angle was modulated by tip-movement direction, creating a baseline TMD-STA (tip-movement direction to stick-tilt angle) relationship. This relationship constrained movement patterns and was achieved by minimizing hand movement distance to near-optimal levels.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these baseline findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 notes 'findings are original and exemplify how baseline relationships determine learning.' Reviewer 2 states participants 'change the tilt angle of the stick in a specific pattern that produces close to minimum movement of the two hands.' The editor confirms 'the evidence supporting the authors' claims is convincing, as demonstrated over four different experiments.'

result: In Experiment 1, when tip-movement direction was perturbed (30° CCW rotation), participants adapted by changing both tip-movement direction and stick-tilt angle. The adaptation followed the baseline TMD-STA relationship, with the adapted pattern resembling voluntary aiming at the -30° target. Individual differences in baseline stick-tilt predicted adapted stick-tilt magnitude.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as demonstrating that 'baseline relationships determine learning' (Reviewer 1). Reviewer 2 notes 'adaptation follows the baseline pattern of tip-movement and stick angle relation.' However, Reviewer 1 requests 'the time course of sensorimotor adaptation' be shown more clearly, suggesting presentation could be improved but not questioning the core findings.

result: In Experiment 2, when only stick-tilt angle was perturbed (±6° around the tip, leaving tip position unchanged), participants still adapted by correcting stick-tilt angle. Unexpectedly, this adaptation was accompanied by undesirable tip-movement direction errors, consistent with the constraint imposed by the baseline TMD-STA relationship.
evaluation: Reviewers found this a key novel finding. Reviewer 2 notes 'even task-irrelevant perturbations drive adaptation in a manner that results in task-relevant errors,' calling this 'an important demonstration.' Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'the nervous system reacts to both types of perturbation' but requests more discussion of 'why adaptation was found in the experiments with end-effector irrelevant' perturbations and how internal models may explain this.

result: The study concludes that implicit adaptation in redundant systems is achieved by two mechanisms: (1) the motor system attempts to correct any perturbation in visual feedback regardless of task relevance, and (2) physical movement correction patterns are constrained by the baseline TMD-STA relationship. This relationship plays a crucial role in both controlling and adapting movements of redundant systems.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted this as a valuable theoretical contribution. The editor states this is 'a valuable finding on how the sensorimotor control system deals with redundancy.' Reviewer 1 notes findings 'exemplify how baseline relationships determine learning.' Reviewer 2 calls it 'an important demonstration that underlying solutions/relations can affect the manner in which we adapt.' However, Reviewer 1 suggests 'the authors may consider modifying the last sentence of the abstract to clearly provide the most substantial theoretical advance.'

result: In Experiment 3, when both tip-movement and stick-tilt perturbations were applied simultaneously, the final adapted movement patterns were similar between groups regardless of stick-tilt perturbation direction. However, adaptation processes differed: tip-movement adaptation was more delayed when the required correction pattern was orthogonal to (rather than aligned with) the baseline TMD-STA relationship.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as supporting the role of baseline relationships in adaptation. Reviewer 2 notes the work 'provides an important demonstration that underlying solutions/relations can affect the manner in which we adapt.' The editor confirms evidence is 'convincing, as demonstrated over four different experiments.' No reviewer challenged the Experiment 3 findings specifically.

result: Experiment 1B (abrupt 30° perturbation allowing explicit strategy) produced nearly identical results to Experiment 1A (gradual perturbation, implicit only), except that the small residual difference in tip-movement direction observed in 1A was absent in 1B. The authors speculate this difference reflects implicit correction of abnormal stick-tilt in Experiment 1A.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 questions whether 'all the necessary evidence appears in this study that control and adaptation are exclusively implicit' and notes 'there is no clear comparison between gradual and abrupt sessions.' The reviewer suggests 'the authors may consider removing at least from the title and abstract the words 'implicit' and 'implicitly.'' This indicates uncertainty about the implicit/explicit distinction and its interpretation.

result: The authors interpret their findings in relation to the minimal intervention principle, suggesting that while Experiment 1 results initially appear consistent with this principle (ignoring task-irrelevant stick-tilt errors), Experiment 2 results contradict it. They propose the motor system corrects end-effector irrelevant errors because: (1) it predicts all sensory consequences and corrects discrepancies, and/or (2) coupled dimensions mean irrelevant errors imply relevant errors.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'the nervous system reacts to both types of perturbation, indicating that they both seem relevant or important' and requests the authors 'extend the Discussion on why adaptation was found in the experiments with end-effector irrelevant and especially how an internal (forward) model or a pair of internal (forward) models may be used to predict both the visual and the somatosensory consequences.' This suggests the theoretical interpretation needs strengthening.

result: The authors acknowledge that experiments were conducted with a specific configuration (stick length, hand distance, target location) and caution about generalizability to other configurations.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly raises this concern: 'The generalizability of the findings is limited. Future work may strengthen the present study's findings by examining whether the observed relationships hold for different stick lengths...or when reaching targets to the left and right of the starting position.' The editor notes 'further investigation into the interpretation of the findings could increase the generalisation of the study to a broader audience.'
